entry.title: Inside Bun’s Runtime: How One Binary Turns Your TypeScript into Running Code

link.title: Inside Bun’s Runtime: How One Binary Turns Your TypeScript into Running Code

entry.content:
You run bun run index.tsx and a file full of TypeScript annotations just executes — no tsconfig.json, no watcher, no compile step you ever invoked. That convenience hides an interesting relay: the type stripping happens inside the import path itself, microseconds before the module’s code reaches the JavaScript engine. What runs between pressing Enter and seeing console.log fire is a four-layer dance between Rust, C++, and JSC.

The other common question is speed. Bun starts noticeably faster than Node.js and bundles a package manager, bundler, test runner, and REPL into one executable. That is several small tricks stacked: a process entry that captures argv before anything allocates, a per-thread VM whose cold-path symbols the linker physically clusters into shared pages, and an event loop without Node’s legacy phases.

This is a source tour of oven-sh/bun at its main branch as of November 2026. First, the repo has drifted from most older descriptions: the Zig implementation is gone — the tree contains zero .zig files — and the runtime is now a workspace of Rust crates with JavaScriptCore reached through C++ bindings. Second, every symbol and line number below was verified by grepping the actual clone. We have done the same treatment for Node.js, and for engines Bun embeds, like SQLite and its Redis protocol client.

One full run of a script: main() hands off to the CLI, which boots a per-thread VirtualMachine; imports flow through JSC's C++ loader into a Rust transpile hook; the run-loop ticks the event loop until idle; FFI callbacks re-enter JS as tasks.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • A C-ABI main, L156 captures argv before anything allocates, installs the crash handler, wires mimalloc as global allocator, and pre-grows Linux fd tables — startup touches each page once.
  • Cli::start, L377 is deliberately #[inline(never)] so lld’s symbol-ordering file can cluster it and its callees into one front-loaded .text run — page-locality engineering at the source level.
  • Run::boot, L972 runs bun_jsc::initialize, then VirtualMachine::init, L1059 returns a leaked, process-lifetime VirtualMachine, L161 that owns the transpiler, module loader, and two event loops by value.
  • Run::start, L1450 takes the JSC API lock and never drops it; its doc comment states the plan plainly: load the entry point, run the event loop until idle, fire exit hooks.
  • Entry loading funnels through load_entry_point, L3915 wrapping reload_entry_point, L3704 — the single funnel for the main entry, workers, and -e evals.
  • JSModuleLoader, L33 is a thin FFI wrapper; real fetch logic lives in JSC’s C++ loader, fetchESMSourceCode, L229, deciding builtins, CommonJS objects, plugins, and file loads.
  • Unseen files cross back into Rust through __bun_transpile_source_code, L2236, documented as: read file, Transpiler::parse, js_printer::print, return ResolvedSource — TypeScript stripping in one line.
  • The core run-loop at L1674 is exactly while vm.is_event_loop_alive() { vm.tick(); vm.auto_tick_active(); } — two calls carrying everything.
  • bun:ffi, L1 closes the circle: dlopen’ed C functions are called directly from JS, and C callbacks come back as event-loop tasks rather than foreign threads poking the engine.

The detail view expands each layer into the concrete functions participating in one import: the boot chain, the JSC C++ fetch decision tree, the parse-and-print transpiler pair, the event loop's queue mechanics, and the TinyCC-backed FFI.

From Boot to a JavaScriptCore VM

The striking thing about the entry path is how much of it is about the linker rather than logic. main marks cold callees #[cold] so LLVM sinks subcommand bodies like bun install to the tail of their translation unit, keeping the bun run chain on hot pages. The comment above main even documents a failed attempt: a two-pass symbol-ordering relink was tried and dropped, because the second link cost more than the layout won.

The VM object reflects strict ownership discipline. VirtualMachine, L161 holds the Transpiler, L39 — described in its own comment as “the JavaScript transpiler before bundle_v2 was written,” now an options-and-resolver object shared with the bundler — plus a ModuleLoader, a RuntimeTranspilerStore cache, and two EventLoop values: regular and macro-mode, with a self-pointer selecting between them. Since EventLoop is a value field of the VM, functions touching both take a raw *mut VirtualMachine and deref per-field — the codebase names this rule after its own PORTING.md “Forbidden” aliasing section.

Embedding JavaScriptCore means speaking two FFI dialects. Rust-to-C++ goes through extern "C" exports like Bun__fetchBuiltinModule; C++-to-Rust uses link-time extern "Rust" declarations — AnyEventLoop, L50 explains that the lower-tier bun_event_loop crate cannot name jsc::EventLoop, so concrete bodies live as #[no_mangle] Rust-ABI functions the linker resolves: “no vtable, no AtomicPtr, and no init-order hazard.” History survives as fossils too — ZigException.rs and a namespace Zig in the C++ headers are seams of the rewrite.

The Import Moment: Resolution and Transpiling

When your file says import { x } from "./util", JSC’s loader asks Bun what to do. fetchESMSourceCode, L229 is the C++ dispatch: builtin specifiers like node:path resolve through Bun__fetchBuiltinModule, L209 against a codegen’d registry; everything else falls to the Rust hook. The loader itself is picked by import type attribute or file extension in Bun__getDefaultLoader, L318 — why .json, .toml, .yaml, or .txt imports work with zero configuration.

The transpile hook is deliberately narrow. __bun_transpile_source_code, L2236 receives TranspileArgs carrying specifier, referrer, loader, and a shared BufferPrinter, L7564 — one per VM, reused across every module. Transpiler::parse runs lexer, parser, and lowering passes and records imports; Transpiler::print emits ordinary JavaScript into the buffer. The ResolvedSource carries printed code and an is_static flag back to C++, which registers and evaluates the module. Second imports short-circuit through the RuntimeTranspilerStore cache instead of re-parsing.

Two details worth noting. The macro event loop exists because Bun macros — compile-time functions invoked with with { type: "macro" } — can do async work during transpilation, so macro mode runs on its own loop instance. And plugin or virtual modules take Bun__transpileVirtualModule, L4946, the same parse-print path fed in-memory contents, hashed per loader and encoding so the cache never collides.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting Bun is a one-liner on every platform, and the README lists them all: the install script (curl -fsSL https://bun.com/install | bash, line 54), powershell -c "irm bun.sh/install.ps1 | iex" for Windows, npm install -g bun, brew install bun, or docker pull oven/bun. Linux, macOS, and Windows are supported on x64 and arm64; Linux kernel 5.6+ is recommended, minimum 5.1.

Building from source is a different weight class, and CONTRIBUTING.md says so in line one: expect 10 to 30 minutes. Prerequisites are unusual for a JavaScript toolchain — Bun is written in Rust and requires a nightly toolchain pinned in rust-toolchain.toml (line 47), plus LLVM 23.1.1, enforced by the build system (line 97). There is a bootstrap quirk: you need a release Bun installed first, because the build uses Bun’s own bundler to transpile the runtime’s JS components (line 53). Clone the repo, run bun run build (line 156), and the debug binary lands at ./build/debug/bun-debug (line 159). Your first run needs no ceremony: bun run index.tsx works in a fresh directory, precisely the import path traced above.

The Event Loop: Two Queues and a Poll Underneath

EventLoop, L48 is a dense struct: a FIFO task queue, two immediate vectors — immediate_tasks for this tick, next_immediate_tasks for the next, exactly to avoid the infinite loop of calling setImmediate inside a setImmediate callback, per the comment at lines 57–65 — plus yield_tasks that asked to run after I/O and timers, concurrent queues for cross-thread posts, and a deferred queue. Everything hangs off a uws_loop handle: the embedded uSockets loop doing the actual polling.

A tick is a bounded refill algorithm. tick, L877 enters a top scope and calls tick_turn, which interleaves tick_with_count (drain tasks), tick_concurrent (take work other threads posted), and a microtask checkpoint via drain_microtasks_and_next_ticks, L179 — process.nextTick callbacks then JSC’s microtask queue, explicitly nothing else, so it cannot re-enter the loop. Refills are capped at CONCURRENT_REFILLS_PER_TICK, so a self-re-posting task cannot starve I/O.

Parking works two ways. auto_tick, L1236 promotes immediates and yields into the task queue and polls while alive; tick_possibly_forever, L1482 is the watcher-arm variant that bounds the park to one second so a cross-thread wakeup() from a --hot reload cannot be missed. A smaller sibling, MiniEventLoop, L65, serves Bun.spawnSync and early boot — initialized globally at L98 before a full VM exists. Native features ride the same queues: the redis preconnect block at L1467 opens a connection to a compatible Valkey server under the API lock, completing as ordinary loop tasks.

Native FFI Without a Build System

bun:ffi takes a different philosophy from Node’s native addons: no node-gyp, no build directory. Function::compile, L646 embeds TinyCC — the file’s use bun_tcc_sys as TCC import sits at line 42 — so new CFunction and cc() compile your C in-process, relocate it, and hand back a callable. The dlopen path at L1531 loads shared libraries on demand.

The type surface is ABIType, with readers and writers for integers, floats, pointers, and C strings. Fast paths are DOMJIT-compiled so reading pointer fields skips a full interpreter call; slowpaths are C-ABI shims in src/runtime/ffi/mod.rs mapping arguments into Rust. The header states the honesty rule plainly: signatures with non-repr(C) types are hard link-time errors, because silent ABI corruption is the classic FFI failure mode. Callbacks are where FFI meets the loop — a C thread invoking JS cannot touch the JSC heap, so the call is posted as a task and runs on the JS thread during a tick.

Honest Limits

  • The runtime is Rust, not Zig, on main. Recent articles describing Bun’s “Zig core” describe a former life: zero .zig files remain, and CONTRIBUTING.md states Bun is written in Rust on a pinned nightly toolchain. C++ still owns the JSC-facing loader and bindings under src/jsc/bindings/.
  • The startup tricks are measured, not magic. The symbol-clustering relink was tried and dropped by the authors as not worth the second link; what remains is #[cold] placement, #[inline(never)] markers, and fd-table pre-growing — each commented with its rationale.
  • bun:ffi’s cc() can be absent. The source contains an explicit error path — “bun:ffi cc() is not available in this build (TinyCC is disabled)” at line 1033 of ffi_body.rs — so trimmed builds lose in-process C compilation while dlopen still works.
  • Transpiling is per-import, per-file. The runtime transpiler handles one module per hook call and caches results, but this path carries no whole-program type checking — only parse and print diagnostics collected in Log.
  • The two-queue immediate design is Node-compatible, not simpler. The comment inside EventLoop says the behavior “is confusing, but that is how it works in Node.js” — compatibility over elegance, on purpose.
entry.summary: A source tour of oven-sh/bun on the main branch, tracing how the Rust runtime embeds JavaScriptCore, transpiles TypeScript at import time, drives the event loop, and wires native FFI.

entry.title: What Actually Happens When You Run python script.py: A CPython Source Tour

link.title: What Actually Happens When You Run python script.py: A CPython Source Tour

entry.content:
Your data-processing loop takes forty seconds while a NumPy rewrite of the same math takes four hundred milliseconds. You profile it, and the answer is not a missing library — it is the interpreter itself. Every attribute lookup, every integer add, every function call in pure Python costs measurable work inside CPython’s C source, and knowing exactly which work it is turns performance guesswork into engineering.

Run python script.py and, somewhere between the shell prompt and your first line, CPython reads your file, lexes it into tokens, runs a PEG grammar to build an AST, lowers that AST through a symbol table into bytecode, and only then hands the bytecode to a dispatch loop that finally executes it. None of this is magic. Each step is a named function you can open and read.

This post walks that execution path through the python/cpython repository on its main branch (commit 8c212aa0de53). Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual tree with grep — no invented names, no stale textbook references.

Overview of CPython's execution path: from Py_BytesMain through the PEG parser and bytecode compiler into the ceval loop, with the specialization tier, dict core, cycle collector, and GIL as services around it.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup begins in Py_BytesMain, L944, which parses argv and hands control to pymain_run_python, L751 — the choke point that decides whether -c, -m, or a file path gets executed.
  • A script flows through pymain_run_file, L488 into _PyRun_File, L1310, which allocates a memory arena, parses, compiles, and executes in one call. The arena is why intermediate parse results stay cheap.
  • Parsing enters at _PyParser_ASTFromFile, L20, which creates tokenizer state via _PyTokenizer_FromFile, L1204 and then drives the generated PEG grammar through _PyPegen_run_parser, L1142 to produce a mod_ty AST.
  • Compilation is two passes: scope analysis in _PySymtable_Build, L423, then instruction emission by compiler_mod, L974 under the _PyAST_Compile, L1683 driver.
  • run_eval_code_obj, L1386 installs __builtins__ into your globals, and PyEval_EvalCode, L612 turns the code object into a frame that _PyEval_Vector, L2158 pushes onto the thread’s frame stack.
  • The frame runs inside _PyEval_EvalFrameDefault, L1204 — one giant dispatch loop whose cases are generated from Python/bytecodes.c and included at ceval.c L1317.
  • Data flow on the hot path lands in dict probes: unicodekeys_lookup_unicode, L1211 is the compact-dict lookup behind global and attribute loads.
  • Control-plane interrupts — signals, GIL handoff, GC requests — all ride the eval_breaker flag checked in the RESUME family at bytecodes.c L152, serviced by handle_eval_breaker, L6654, gc_collect_main, L1431, and take_gil, L286.

Detail view: the full call chain from Modules/main.c into Python/pythonrun.c, Parser/peg_api.c, Python/compile.c, and Python/ceval.c, plus the bytecode families, specialization hooks, refcounting, and the GC and GIL services.

From Source to Bytecode

The tokenizer is now a layered subsystem. _PyPegen_run_parser_from_file_pointer in pegen.c L1198 creates a tok_state over your file stream, and the lexer itself lives under Parser/lexer/ — see the character-level scanner _PyLexer_get_normal at lexer.c L121. Tokens feed the PEG parser: _PyPegen_run_parser at pegen.c L1142 runs the grammar tables generated from Grammar/python.gram, and when parsing fails, error recovery in Parser/pegen_errors.c builds the precise SyntaxError you see in the console.

The AST then crosses into the compiler. _PyRun_File allocates the scratch arena first — _PyArena_New, L1317 — so every AST node allocated during parsing lives in pooled memory that is freed wholesale once compilation finishes. _PyAST_Compile, L1683 then builds the symbol table — _PySymtable_Build, L423 walks every scope and decides which names are locals, globals, or cells — and only then emits instructions. Statement lowering is compiler_mod, L974, which recursively visits the mod_ty tree and writes instruction sequences with resolved jump targets.

One modern detail worth knowing: the bytecode itself is declared in Python/bytecodes.c as a DSL. Families like BINARY_OP, L618, LOAD_GLOBAL, L2222, and CALL, L4296 are transpiled into the C switch cases that ceval includes. That single source of truth is also what generates the tier-2 micro-op set used by the JIT under Python/jit.c.

Inside ceval: One Giant Loop

_PyEval_EvalFrameDefault, L1204 is the beating heart. Depending on build flags it either uses computed gotos or the newer tail-call interpreter style — both are visible as #if branches around the dispatch code. The actual per-opcode cases arrive from generated_cases.c.h, included at ceval.c L1317, so the loop you read in ceval.c is the scaffold and bytecodes.c is the meat.

Every instruction reads from a value stack of _PyStackRef entries, and each opcode carries inline cache slots right in the bytecode stream. The first time a generic opcode like BINARY_OP executes on new operand types, it calls _Py_Specialize_BinaryOp, L2339, which rewrites the instruction in place into a type-specific variant such as BINARY_OP_ADD_INT. The same pattern covers global loads via _Py_Specialize_LoadGlobal, L1457 and calls via _Py_Specialize_Call, L1872. This is the adaptive part of the specializing interpreter, and it is why a hot loop gets measurably faster after its first few iterations.

Interruptions are cheap because the loop checks a single atomic flag. The _CHECK_PERIODIC opcode at bytecodes.c L159 compares tstate->eval_breaker against a cached version; when a signal, a trace event, or a GIL handoff is pending, control funnels into handle_eval_breaker at bytecodes.c L6654. Calls are equally tuned: CALL_PY_EXACT_ARGS, L4619 enters the callee frame directly when arity matches, skipping the generic argument-parsing machinery. Function exits are just as explicit: RETURN_VALUE, L1592 moves the return value, pops the frame, and resumes the caller’s instruction pointer. For very hot code, _PyOptimizer_Optimize, L1049 is the doorway into tier 2, where traces of micro-ops get built and, in JIT builds, compiled to machine code.

Objects, Refcounts, and the Cycle Collector

CPython’s memory model starts with one rule: every PyObject carries a type pointer and a reference count, and ownership is manual. The increment itself is Py_INCREF, L255, an atomic operation that also encodes immortality — objects whose counter reaches the thresholds documented around refcount.h L44 are treated as permanent and skip future refcount traffic. This is why refcounts dominate the runtime: a dict lookup inside unicodekeys_lookup_unicode, L1211 or a list growth inside list_resize, L111 is continuously bumping counters.

Refcounting cannot reclaim cycles, so containers take a different allocation route. _PyObject_GC_New at gc.c L2047 goes through gc_alloc, L2027, which links the new object into generational lists. When allocation thresholds trip, gc_collect_main, L1431 runs deduce_unreachable, L1168, a mark pass over the young generation that finds objects reachable only through cycles. The dict layout itself is documented at the top of dictobject.c L28: a dense dk_indices table pointing into an ordered entries array, which is what makes those probes cache-friendly and keeps insertion order. That is the entire conceptual gap between “garbage” and “cycle garbage” — and it is why small ints, interned strings, and function defaults are cheap while huge interlinked object graphs cost collection time.

The GIL: One Lock to Rule the Loop

The GIL exists because the design above assumes exactly one thread is executing bytecode per interpreter at a time. Threads coordinate through take_gil, L286 and drop_gil, L217: a thread that has run for its switch interval sets the eval_breaker, the running loop notices it at the next periodic check, drops the lock, and a waiting thread wakes to take it. The shared state lives in struct _gil_runtime_state, passed straight into drop_gil_impl, L203, so the drop-request protocol is readable in a single screen of C. C-level releases happen around blocking I/O so that network threads never stall the interpreter — the mechanism behind everything from Flask request handling to FastAPI worker pools.

The tree already carries the no-GIL path. Python/gc_free_threading.c sits next to Python/gc.c, and ceval.c guards thread-local bytecode with Py_GIL_DISABLED conditionals. In a free-threaded build the per-object locking strategy changes, which is exactly why the immortal-reference encoding in refcount.h matters: it removes shared-counter writes for objects that can never be freed.

From Install to Your First Model

Building CPython from this tree is deliberately boring. On Linux and macOS the documented path in README.rst L53 is ./configure, make, make test, and sudo make install; a debug build passes --with-pydebug to configure as shown at README.rst L87. On Windows the entry point is the PCbuild solution, linked from README.rst L76. Passing --enable-optimizations to configure turns on profile-guided optimization before make (README.rst L94), and note that ceval.c contains MSVC-specific PGO pragmas precisely because the eval loop is the hottest function in the binary.

Once installed, your first model is a two-liner: pip install scikit-learn, then fit a LinearRegression on a few hundred rows. Every step of that fit — the Python loop over features, the dict lookups for attribute access, the calls into compiled BLAS code — runs through the exact chain in the diagrams above, from Py_BytesMain down to the eval loop handing off to C extensions when LangChain-style tools or ORM-heavy Django views call into NumPy-backed code.

Honest Limits

Everything cited here is a snapshot of main at commit 8c212aa0de53 — line numbers drift fast on this repo, so re-grep before quoting them elsewhere. The free-threading and JIT paths are build-time options, not defaults: whether Python/jit.c or Python/gc_free_threading.c is active depends entirely on the configure flags your binary was built with. The tier-2 optimizer interfaces (Python/optimizer.c, Python/optimizer_analysis.c) are still evolving, and the bytecode DSL in Python/bytecodes.c is regenerated rather than edited by hand — do not patch generated files. Finally, this tour follows one execution path; import machinery, async generators, and the C extension protocol are whole subsystems of their own, and the framework source tours of FastAPI and Flask only make sense once you know the interpreter they ride on.
entry.summary: A verified walk through CPython's main branch: tokenizer, PEG parser, bytecode compiler, the ceval dispatch loop, refcounting, the cycle collector, and the GIL.

entry.title: Inside Deno: How a Rust Core Hosts V8 and Guards Every Op

link.title: Inside Deno: How a Rust Core Hosts V8 and Guards Every Op

entry.content:
You write await fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/models") in TypeScript and a response comes back. But between that one line and the network card there is a boundary most JavaScript developers never see: the call leaves V8’s world of heap objects and hidden classes and enters a Rust program that owns the socket, the TLS state machine, and the event loop. What actually crosses that line? A small integer op id, a promise id, and a handful of marshalled arguments. Everything else — buffering, cancellation, timers — is Rust code waiting on a Tokio future that your JavaScript knows nothing about.

The second invisible mechanism is the permission prompt. When you run deno run --allow-net=api.github.com main.ts and the script touches another host, you get a terminal prompt asking for --allow-net=api.openai.com. That is not a runtime library wrapper or a monkey-patched fetch. It is a check executed inside the op implementation itself, in Rust, before the request is ever built: op_fetch in the fetch extension borrows PermissionsContainer from OpState and calls check_net_url(&url, "fetch()") at line 479 of ext/fetch/lib.rs. If you granted nothing, the prompt fires from the same code path. There is no way for user JavaScript to reach the socket without walking through that check, because there is no other door to the socket.

And why did Deno choose V8 plus Rust in the first place? Because the architecture is a classic embedder split, the same shape you see when CPython embeds native extensions or when Rust web servers like Actix Web park thousands of futures on a few threads. V8 executes JS and JITs it well; Rust owns everything V8 cannot do — sockets, files, crypto, process spawning — and a thin, generated bridge glues the two. The result is a runtime where every Web API is really an op registration plus a Rust function, and where the entire event loop is a Future polled from Tokio.

This post is a source tour of the denoland/deno repository, main branch, as of 2026-11-10. Every symbol, file, and line number below was verified against the actual tree with grep before publication — note that the core recently moved from a top-level core/ directory into libs/core/ and the op macro into libs/ops/, so older write-ups citing core/ops.rs are pointing at a layout that no longer exists.

The boot path from `cli/main.rs` down to `JsRuntime`, with the op bridge and permission boundary that every Web API call must cross. Generated from the verified denoland/deno source graph.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The binary’s main is deliberately trivial — main, L3 only calls deno::main(), so the real boot — panic hook, logging, fd limits, prompt callbacks, V8 platform init — lives in main, L859. The comment there explains that V8’s platform must be initialized on the parent thread of every isolate thread.
  • Startup speed comes from a snapshot, not from re-parsing JS at launch: CLI_SNAPSHOT, L4 embeds a precompiled V8 heap blob via include_bytes!, produced at build time by create_runtime_snapshot, L50 from all extension sources.
  • The user-facing handle is MainWorker, L194, constructed through bootstrap_from_options, L441 and a shared common_runtime, L1282 factory that fills a 20-field RuntimeOptions struct.
  • JsRuntime, L456 is the heart: one Rust struct owning one V8 isolate, its realms, allocations, and the module map. It exposes execute_script, mod_evaluate, and the event loop your program lives on.
  • Extensions are wired by lazy_init_extensions, L612, which passes per-extension args for web, fetch, cache, websocket, crypto, net, kv, ffi, http, io, fs, and os into the core registry — this is where Deno.fetch becomes real code.
  • Each realm carries its own op driver: the alias at OpDriverImpl, L64 resolves to FuturesUnorderedDriver, which parks in-flight async op futures until the event loop polls them.
  • The op boundary is generated code: the op2, L25 proc macro expands ordinary Rust functions into fast-call capable dispatchers, with each call receiving an OpCtx, L102 carrying the op id, declaration pointer, and shared state.
  • Permissions ride along as ordinary state: ops borrow PermissionsContainer, L4132 from OpState, so a network op cannot run without a check happening inside Rust.
  • Module loading is pluggable: CliModuleLoader, L1322 implements the core ModuleLoader, L61 trait, feeding the module graph, npm resolution, and load hooks into the isolate.

The detail view follows one fetch call and one module load end to end: extension registration, the op2-generated dispatcher, the FuturesUnordered op driver, the Rust-to-JS `__eventLoopTick` callback, and the permission prompter. Same verified source graph, one level deeper.

Two Layers, One Isolate

JsRuntime::new at new, L756 takes the RuntimeOptions the worker built — module loader, startup snapshot, extensions, inspector flag — and creates the V8 isolate. After construction, Rust reaches into JavaScript exactly once to wire callbacks: store_js_callbacks, L1703 grabs Deno.core.__eventLoopTick, __processTimers, and __drainNextTickAndMacrotasks from the global Deno object as v8::Function handles. Those three functions are the entire reverse channel: Rust will later call back into them to resolve promises and run timers.

The JS side of core lives in 01_core.js, where __eventLoopTick at L461 consumes (promiseId, isOk, res) triples and settles the matching promise. This is why Deno’s microtask ordering is explicit: op resolution defers microtask checkpoints, and Rust drives the drain separately. Meanwhile the bootstrap script bootstrapMainRuntime, L936 installs the Deno namespace, sets up globals, then deletes globalThis.bootstrap so embedder internals stop being reachable.

The event loop itself is honest about what it is: run_event_loop, L2321 is a poll_fn over poll_event_loop, L2390, and its doc comment promises it will not resolve while dynamic imports, pending ops, or inspector sessions remain. Your whole program is one future that Tokio polls until everything drains.

The Op Bridge: From JavaScript Call to Rust Future

Every Web API operation is declared as a Rust function annotated with #[op2], and the proc macro at op2, L25 generates the machinery: argument extraction from V8 fast API calling conventions, a slow fallback path, and for async ops a submit wrapper. The extension declaration in the fetch crate shows the pattern — deno_core::extension!, L159 lists op_fetch, op_fetch_send, op_fetch_custom_client, and friends plus eight lazy-loaded JS files that define the standard fetch() surface.

When an async op runs, map_async_op_infallible, L36 turns the Rust future into a driver submission. The OpDriver, L52 trait’s submit_op_infallible at L56 parks the future inside FuturesUnorderedDriver at FuturesUnorderedDriver, L56, keyed by promise id. Nothing in user JavaScript ever blocks: the op returns a promise immediately, and the driver’s results are batched back into __eventLoopTick when the event loop next polls.

Sync ops take the fast path: V8’s fast API calls let a compiled JS function invoke the Rust function directly without leaving machine code, which is why #[op2] exists at all. The macro decides per-op whether fast calls are legal based on the signature, falling back to the slow path when arguments get exotic. If you have read about how Node or Bun schedule their native bindings, this is the same shape — but here the binding layer is a generated Rust dispatcher, and it is shared by every extension from fetch to FFI.

Permissions Are Just Another Type in OpState

OpState at OpState, L395 is a typed bag: resources, timers, extension options, and the permission container all live there. An op that wants the network does state.borrow::<PermissionsContainer>() and checks. In the fetch op at op_fetch, L436, the scheme is inspected before the permission check — file: URLs route to a file fetch handler, and only http/https reach check_net_url, L4753 with the api name "fetch()" at L479. TCP is equally guarded: op_net_connect_tcp at op_net_connect_tcp, L589 calls check_net with the resolved host and port at L624.

The container itself wraps Permissions at L3689 behind an Arc<Mutex<...>>, with per-verb UnaryPermission types. The read check at check, L3225 audits and delegates to check_desc, and when nothing is granted the prompter is consulted: permission_prompt, L99 renders the TTY allow/deny prompt. Because checks happen inside op implementations, worker boundaries and child permissions funnel through the same container — there is exactly one place to audit.

Module Loading: From URL to V8 Module

The core defines what a loader must do — ModuleLoader, L61 with resolve and load — but the CLI owns the real implementation. CliModuleLoader::load at load, L1428 returns a ModuleLoadResponse and can delegate to JS load hooks asynchronously when they are registered; prepare_load at L1611 drives graph prefetch. Execution starts at execute_main_module, L989, which loads the entry module and then races module evaluation against the event loop in evaluate_module, L934 using tokio::select! with biased mode — the comment notes that bias matters for determinism.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one command per platform, straight from the repository README: curl -fsSL https://deno.land/install.sh | sh on Mac and Linux, irm https://deno.land/install.ps1 | iex on Windows, plus Homebrew, Chocolatey, WinGet, and Scoop variants. Building from source is a Rust toolchain exercise; the README points to the contributing guide’s “Building from source” section, and the workspace Cargo.toml shows the member crates you would compile — cli, ext/*, and libs/* including libs/core and libs/ops.

Your first program needs no package install at all. Create server.ts with Deno.serve((_req: Request) => new Response("Hello, world!")) and run deno run --allow-net server.ts — the README’s exact example, served at localhost:8000. The same zero-install property is what makes a first LLM call trivial: a script that does await fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/models") uses the exact op_fetch path described above, needing only --allow-net=api.openai.com. Compare that with the Node.js and Bun ecosystems where an HTTP client package usually arrives before line one — the capability you are granting is visible on the command line before the code runs.

Honest Limits

Three things worth knowing before you cite internals. First, the layout is in motion: core/ became libs/core/, the op macro became libs/ops/, and the permissions crate lives at runtime/permissions/ — any tutorial citing the old paths describes a tree that no longer exists on main, and line numbers in this post will drift the day after publish. Second, fast calls are an optimization, not a guarantee: the op2 macro ships both dispatch_fast.rs and dispatch_slow.rs, and ops with exotic signatures always take the slow path, so “zero-cost binding” is directionally true, not literally true. Third, the permission model guards access through ops, which is precisely why it is effective for files, network, and environment — but the fetch op checks the URL scheme before the net check, meaning file: fetches are permission-gated by the read permission path instead of net. Deno’s own code comments make these boundaries explicit; trust the source, not the marketing.
entry.summary: A source tour of denoland/deno showing how JsRuntime embeds V8, how the op2 bridge turns JavaScript calls into Rust futures, and where permission checks actually run.

entry.title: Inside the Go Runtime: How G/M/P, Channels, and the Tricolor GC Actually Run Your Code

link.title: Inside the Go Runtime: How G/M/P, Channels, and the Tricolor GC Actually Run Your Code

entry.content:
Every Go developer has felt the gap. You write go handler(conn) and the function starts running on a stack measured in kilobytes — tens of thousands of them per process, on the same machine where a Python program threads awkwardly around the GIL. In CPython, a thread is an OS thread with a lock around bytecode execution; in Go, concurrency is a runtime-internal illusion layered on top of a small number of real threads. That gap is not magic. It is roughly eight thousand lines of exacting Go code in src/runtime/proc.go, and understanding it changes how you write servers — the same discipline that powers gin, etcd, and kubernetes.

The pain shows up in production telemetry. Why does p99 latency jump right when a channel’s buffer fills and senders start parking? Why does the GC steal CPU from your hot handler even though the world is never fully stopped? Why does a goroutine blocked on a socket cost nothing, while one spinning in a tight loop is preempted exactly 10 milliseconds later? Each question has a precise answer in the runtime source — the scheduler’s spinning-thread protocol, the GC pacer’s assist mechanism, and one constant called forcePreemptNS.

This post tours the actual implementation. The target is the golang/go repository on GitHub, branch master, and every symbol, file, and line number cited below was grepped and verified against a real checkout of that tree — no invented identifiers, no stale blog-lore. Two diagrams map the territory: an overview of the execution path from go build to a running goroutine, and a detailed graph of the scheduler, channel, allocator, GC, netpoller, and stack machinery.

Overview of the Go execution path: the toolchain produces a binary whose entry point is the runtime, the runtime boots the G/M/P scheduler, and channel, allocation, and GC operations all funnel back into the same scheduling loop.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The binary starts in the runtime, not your code. CmdBuild, L29 drives the build, but the linked executable’s real entry point is runtime.main, L152, which first runs schedinit, L843 to bootstrap the allocator, GC, and the array of Ps.
  • go statements are allocations, not syscalls. newproc, L5341 creates a new g via newproc1 and hands it to runqput, L7550, which fills the P’s runnext slot; runqputslow, L7596 spills half the queue to the global one only when the 256-slot ring overflows.
  • Scheduling is P-first, then global, then theft. schedule, L4157 calls findRunnable, L3409, which tries the local queue, the global run queue via globrunqget, L7353, GC mark workers, and finally stealWork, L3848 — stealing half a victim P’s queue in one batch with runqgrab, L7734.
  • Blocking never blocks the thread. chansend, L168 hands its value straight to a parked receiver or buffers it; on a full buffer it enqueues a sudog and calls gopark, L456, and the same thread is instantly back in schedule looking for other work.
  • Allocation is almost lock-free. mallocgc, L1016 serves small objects from a per-P mcache; mcache.refill, L160 pulls a fresh span from the mheap.central, L211 lists only when the local span is exhausted.
  • The GC rides the scheduler instead of pausing it. gcStart, L733 flips the heap into _GCmark and enables the write barrier; gcBgMarkWorker, L1766 goroutines are handed to Ps by findRunnableGCWorker, so marking competes fairly with user goroutines rather than monopolizing cores.
  • Wakeups converge on the same queues. goready, L492 (backed by ready, L1122) is the single re-entry point: a finished syscall, a ready socket, or a completed channel send all end with a G dropped onto some P’s run queue.

The detailed graph follows one coherent execution path — spawn, schedule, block on a channel, allocate, trigger GC, and wake through the netpoller — with every node pinned to a verified line in the master tree.

Goroutines Are Not Threads: The G/M/P Machine

Three structs carry the whole design. g, L471 is a goroutine: stack bounds, a status field cycling through runnable, running, and waiting, and a saved register buffer. m, L615 is an OS thread with its own g0 scheduling stack. p, L774 is the crucial middle layer — a scheduler context owning a local run queue, an mcache, and timers. An M must hold a P to execute Go code; work therefore lands on a P first, and only contention pushes it global, onto schedt, L936.

The fairness machinery lives outside the scheduler loop entirely. sysmon, L6550 is a thread that runs without a P, waking between 20 microseconds and 10 milliseconds; its retake, L6694 pass does two jobs. If an M has been stuck in a syscall past a sysmon tick, the P is handed off via handoffp, L3141 to a fresh thread. If a goroutine has occupied the same P past forcePreemptNS — a 10-millisecond constant defined at proc.go, L6692 — preemptone, L6930 forces it out, which is why an untight loop can never starve its siblings. When a goroutine finally returns, goexit0, L4513 resets it to _Gdead and returns the thread to schedule; spawning an M (newm, proc.go, L2870) happens only when idle Ps actually need threads.

When a Channel Blocks: sudog, sendq, and gopark

A channel is a small struct, not a queue library. hchan, L34 holds a circular buffer with send and receive indexes, two waiter lists, and — remarkably — a single lock. The send path in chansend, L168 has three outcomes. First, if a receiver is already parked on recvq, send (chan.go, L310) copies the value directly into the receiver’s stack slot and marks it runnable — the buffered channel memory is bypassed entirely. Second, if buffer space exists, the value lands at sendx and the lock is released; the whole fast path costs one mutex acquire.

Only the third outcome blocks, and it does so without blocking the thread. The sender allocates a sudog, L404 — the runtime’s record of “one goroutine waiting on one channel” — via acquireSudog, L499, enqueues it on sendq at chan.go, L265, and calls gopark. The M is immediately free; when a receiver or closechan, L406 completes the operation, the parked G re-enters the normal queues. The mirror image lives in chanrecv, L516, where a waiting sender’s value is stolen via sendDirect (chan.go, L384). One subtlety: parkingOnChan and chanparkcommit, L741 exist so the stack-shrink machinery never moves a stack out from under a parked sudog.

The Allocator and the Stacks Beneath It

mallocgc is a size dispatcher. Tiny no-scan objects under 16 bytes go to mallocgcTiny, L1153, which packs several small strings into one 8-byte block; medium objects split between mallocgcSmallNoscan, L1309 and two scan-aware paths; anything large goes straight to mallocgcLarge, L1638 and the heap. The per-P mcache (mcache.go, L48) caches exactly one span per size class, and the class count is NumSizeClasses << 1 — scan and no-scan variants (mheap.go, L576). That is why allocation on a busy multi-core server rarely touches a shared lock: the P-local span absorbs it.

Goroutine stacks follow the same “pay for what you use” philosophy. A new G starts on a small stack from stackalloc, L344; on overflow, newstack, L1067 allocates a doubled stack and adjustframe, L701 rewrites every pointer in every frame during the copy. Oversized stacks are reclaimed at GC time by shrinkstack, L1298. This is why deeply recursive code can be as cheap in Go as iterative code — the runtime quietly moves your stack between the OS pages.

The Tricolor GC and Your p99

The collector is concurrent, tricolor mark-sweep with a hybrid write barrier. gcStart, L733 begins with a very short stop-the-world window that only switches the phase to _GCmark and enables the write barrier (mgc.go, L259); application goroutines resume immediately after. Marking itself is spread across per-P workers: gcBgMarkWorker, L1766 loops forever, and the scheduler hands workers out through findRunnableGCWorker (mgcpacer.go, L859) — GC work literally competes with your goroutines inside findRunnable, which is the design’s central trick.

The actual marking is a work-stealing traversal. gcDrain, L1253 pulls grey objects from a local gcWork buffer; markroot, L221 scans globals and every goroutine stack (scanstack, L904); scanblock, L1493 follows pointers and greyobject, L1653 shades discovered objects. If allocation outpaces the background workers, the mutator pays: gcAssistAlloc, L499 makes the allocating goroutine do scan work proportional to the bytes it allocated. That assist — not a monolithic pause — is what produces those small p99 wobbles under allocation pressure, and it is why the pacer’s heap goal (gcPercentHeapGoal, L149) matters for latency tuning. gcMarkDone, L997 closes the mark phase, and bgsweep, L285 reclaims spans lazily in the background. Note also that forcegcperiod, L6540 forces a cycle every two minutes even if the heap goal is never reached — a quiet source of periodic latency in allocation-light services.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository’s own README keeps it simple: official binary distributions are available at go.dev/dl/, with installation instructions linked from the docs, and for unsupported platform combinations the source-install instructions live at go.dev/doc/install/source. The canonical Git repository is hosted at go.googlesource.com/go, with github.com/golang/go acting as the read-only mirror this tour used. The Go source is distributed under a BSD-style license found in the repo’s LICENSE file.

From source to a running program, the toolchain is entirely self-hosted. The go command’s build path is implemented in src/cmd/go/internal/work — CmdBuild, L29 with runBuild at L465 — and each package is compiled by cmd/compile, whose Main, L67 wires inlining and escape analysis before the SSA backend takes over at buildssa, L302. The SSA pass table, from initial deadcode elimination through lower to lowered cse, is declared in compile.go, L414. The mental model to carry into your first concurrent program: the compiler emits the code, but the runtime you now understand decides when, where, and on which stack it runs.

Honest Limits

This tour is deliberately narrow. The scheduler code shown here is the mainstream path in proc.go; OS specifics leak through — extra stack headroom is added only on Windows and Plan 9 (stack.go, L75). The netpoller’s actual event loop is implemented per OS — epoll, kqueue, IOCP — outside the generic netpoll.go we touched, so its internals deserve a separate tour. Line numbers are pinned to the master tree as of this writing and will drift; the symbols, not the numbers, are the durable knowledge. And whole subsystems remain unopened: timer heaps (checkTimers), cgo transitions, the trace reader, and the pacer’s control theory in mgcpacer.go.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of the golang/go runtime showing how the G/M/P scheduler, channel blocking, tricolor garbage collector, and per-P memory allocator execute every goroutine you spawn.

entry.title: How Node.js Actually Runs Your Code: Bootstrap, the Event Loop, and the Thread Pool in the Source

link.title: How Node.js Actually Runs Your Code: Bootstrap, the Event Loop, and the Thread Pool in the Source

entry.content:
Every Node.js developer eventually meets the same wall: one synchronous call — a tight JSON parse, a CPU-bound transform, a blocking hash — and the whole server freezes. Requests queue, timers slip, health checks fail. The usual explanation, “JavaScript is single-threaded,” is true but useless; it doesn’t tell you what is actually stuck or why async code is the fix. The real answer lives in the C++ layer under your require().

The second mystery is the event loop. It gets drawn as a diagram with six colored boxes, as if it were a scheduler Node ships. It isn’t. It is one C function, uv_run, inside libuv — a library Node vendors into its own tree — and the phases people talk about are the literal statements of a while loop in that function. Once you read it, setTimeout vs setImmediate ordering, process.nextTick semantics, and why the process exits when handlers finish all stop being folklore.

The third puzzle is the thread pool. If JavaScript runs on one thread, who does the blocking? File reads, DNS-style lookups and similar work vanish into a small set of worker threads — four by default — managed by libuv, with their completions funneled back into the loop you already understand. This post tours the actual execution path in the nodejs/node repository on the main branch: every file, symbol, and line number below was grepped and verified against the real tree, not reconstructed from blog posts.

Overview: the five stages between your terminal and your code — C++ bootstrap, JS bootstrap, module loading, the libuv event loop, and the worker thread pool that absorbs blocking I/O.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The whole runtime is an embedded V8 program. On Unix, main, L96 is essentially return node::Start(argc, argv) — nothing else happens before it.
  • Start, L1848 delegates to StartInternal, L1776, which does process-global setup once: argument fixing, InitializeOncePerProcessInternal, L1783, and configuring the default loop with idle-time metrics at uv_loop_configure, L1806.
  • The per-process work ends by constructing a NodeMainInstance::Run, L89 over uv_default_loop(), which calls CreateMainEnvironment at L126 — deserializing a build-time startup snapshot, or making a fresh context.
  • JS core loads before any user code: LoadEnvironment, L597 triggers Realm::RunBootstrapping, L190, which executes internal/bootstrap/realm.js, home of the BuiltinModule, L245 registry that backs internalBinding().
  • Standard streams are wired by probing file descriptors: guessHandleType, L53 switches on TTY/FILE/PIPE/TCP to decide what stdout actually is.
  • One of the main scripts in lib/internal/main is selected by C++, and prepareMainThreadExecution, L49 applies run-time state (CLI options, argv expansion) before anything user-owned runs.
  • The entry point goes through the CommonJS loader’s public face first: run_main_module.js calls Module.runMain, which is aliased at L520 to executeUserEntryPoint, L146.
  • That loader decision is deliberate: unless shouldUseESMLoader, L53 says otherwise, the entry is attempted as CommonJS via wrapModuleLoad at L173, with an ESM retry path for ambiguous files.
  • After the entry runs, control never returns to the “end of script”: NodeMainInstance::Run spins SpinEventLoopInternal, L23, a do/while that alternates uv_run, L427 with NodePlatform::DrainTasks, L579 until the loop dies.

The detail view adds the binding layer, both module loaders, the timer round-trip between C++ and JS, the fs-to-threadpool path, and per-worker loops.

A Bootstrap You Can Trace in Two Files

The C++ side is remarkably linear. src/node_main.cc is a thin shell; src/node.cc holds the real sequence. StartInternal sets up process state once per process, then the interesting choice: CreateMainEnvironment, L126 either reads the context out of an embedded V8 startup snapshot or builds a new one. The snapshot is real — lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js documents at L7-L16 that its heap is captured by node_mksnapshot at build time, and passing --no-node-snapshot makes Node actually execute that script on each start.

Inside the realm bootstrap, lib/internal/bootstrap/realm.js installs the built-in module machinery and the internalBinding() bridge; lib/internal/bootstrap/node.js then sets up the global and process objects in a deliberately synchronous, environment-independent way. Only after that do the switches/ scripts run, wiring stdio based on what the descriptor turns out to be. This two-layer split explains a subtle fact: code in the bootstrap phase must not perform async operations, which is exactly why your first I/O doesn’t happen until lib/internal/main scripts take over.

The Binding Layer: How C++ Exposes Itself to JS

There is no magic require for native code at this level — there is a registry. GetInternalBinding, L997 hands JS the exports object of a compiled-in native module, and RegisterExternalReferences, L1083 is where each subsystem registers its callbacks with the V8 external-reference table so they can be fast-called.

Timers show the round-trip crisply. JS calls internalBinding('timers') (lib/internal/timers.js L85) and hands C++ two functions through SetupTimers (src/timers.cc). When a libuv timer expires, Environment::RunTimers, L1773 — started via uv_timer_start at L1760 — invokes the stored callback, which is JS’s processTimers, L596. Your setTimeout callback therefore enters your code from inside a C function that libuv scheduled; that is the entire “magic.”

The Event Loop Is a C Function with Seven Phases

Open uv_run, L427 and the diagram becomes code. After checking uv__loop_alive, a while loop at L445 runs: pending callbacks, idle handles, prepare handles, then uv__io_poll, L460 with a computed timeout, then check and closing handles, then uv__run_timers, L478. The “phases” are just these calls in order.

Node wraps this: SpinEventLoopInternal, L23 repeatedly calls uv_run and DrainTasks, L579 — which flushes V8 platform foreground tasks for the isolate (FlushForegroundTasksInternal, L607) — then checks uv_loop_alive and emits beforeExit for a last chance to keep living. The process exits when nothing alive remains: no open handles, no pending timers, no unsettled promises the loop cares about.

CommonJS or ESM: The Decision at Startup

For node entry.js, lib/internal/main/run_main_module.js ends with Module.runMain(mainEntry), which is aliased at L520 to executeUserEntryPoint — so even ESM entries enter through the CJS loader’s public surface, a compatibility choice documented in that file. shouldUseESMLoader, L53 checks extension and package type; when ESM wins, importForEntryPoint, L184 drives ESMLoader.import, L682, returning a promise only when top-level await is involved.

CommonJS loading itself is Module._load, L1341: a per-directory relative-resolve cache for fast repeats, a Module._cache hit path, circular-dependency handling that returns partial exports, and hook-aware resolution. The cache is why require is idempotent per file — and why a module that throws can leave a half-initialized entry behind.

The Thread Pool: Where Blocking Work Actually Goes

libuv keeps a small worker pool: default_threads, L39 has four entries, sized from UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE at L207, capped at 1024. Work is submitted through uv_queue_work, L379; completions wake the loop. Node’s file layer rides on this: every uv_fs_* operation executes in uv__fs_work, L1679 and is submitted via uv__work_submit, and src/node_file.cc dispatches async reads with uv_fs_read at L637.

Streams sit on top of these handles. Readable, L344 with Readable.prototype.read, L700 implements push/pull with backpressure buffers — the reason piping a large response doesn’t balloon memory. For concurrency beyond one isolate, worker_threads spawn real OS threads via uv_thread_create_ex, L781, and each worker runs its own SpinEventLoopInternal, L438. If you embed a synchronous local store like SQLite in-process, its speed profile is yours to manage — the pool will not absorb it for you.

From Install to Your First Model

Building Node from source is ordinary autotools-style work, fully documented in the repo. From a clone of nodejs/node, the canonical sequence is ./configure followed by make -j4 (BUILDING.md, L359-L360); expect roughly 8 GB of RAM when compiling with four parallel jobs (L243), and a g++ or clang compatible with C++20 (L366). make -j4 test runs the full check suite including documentation tests (L412).

The resulting ./node binary is everything above in one executable. Your first run — say a script that calls a hosted LLM endpoint or streams tokens to the console — exercises the exact path in this tour: main → StartInternal → snapshot deserialize → bootstrap realm → executeUserEntryPoint → uv_run. Node itself ships no model runtime; it is a JS host, so anything LLM-flavored arrives as npm dependencies, or as frameworks built on it like Express and Hono. The Python-minded can compare this whole bootstrap story with CPython, where the interpreter loop and GIL play the roles libuv and the isolate play here.

Honest Limits

  • One isolate, one loop. A synchronous call blocks its own isolate’s event loop — the fix spaces are: move work to the pool (libuv-managed only), to a worker thread, or to another process. The pool does not rescue unbounded JS computation; it only carries submitted libuv work such as the fs path shown above.
  • Pool defaults are small on purpose: four workers (L39), tunable via UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE up to 1024. A full audit of which Node subsystems use the pool versus dedicated threads was out of scope here — the fs path is verified end-to-end; crypto and DNS internals were not traced in this tour.
  • Bootstrap JS mostly doesn’t run at startup: it is deserialized from the build-time snapshot (L13), so profiling “cold start” with --no-node-snapshot measures a different program than production.
  • This tour follows the Unix execution path; libuv ships a parallel Windows implementation in deps/uv/src/win/core.c, and the phase machine there is a separate file. Ordering rules that developers feel — timers, immediates, next-ticks — also live partly in JS (lib/internal/timers.js) and partly in C++, so “one source of truth” for ordering claims doesn’t exist in a single file.
entry.summary: A verified walk through the nodejs/node tree — from int main() through V8 bootstrap, the binding layer, CommonJS/ESM loading, libuv's phase machine, and the 4-worker thread pool.

entry.title: Inside php-src: How PHP Actually Runs Your Code, from SAPI to the Zend VM

link.title: Inside php-src: How PHP Actually Runs Your Code, from SAPI to the Zend VM

entry.content:
Every PHP developer eventually meets the same mystery: you edit a file, refresh, and the change is live — yet the code runs fast enough to serve thousands of requests per second. That only makes sense once you realize PHP compiles your script on every request, and that OPcache exists precisely to stop the waste. The shared-nothing model — no persistent in-process state between HTTP requests — makes deploys trivial and bugs die with the request, but it also means the engine repeats enormous work unless something intervenes.

And a lot happens before your first line runs. A server component hands the request to the engine through a C function-table contract, the engine boots (or reuses) its state, allocates an interpreter stack, activates every extension, and only then opens your file. That boundary — what happens once per process versus once per request — explains half of PHP’s operational behavior, from memory limits to why long-running workers drifted so far from the classic model.

This post is a source tour of the php/php-src repository on the master branch (as of November 2026), the tree that builds the engine behind everything from a shared host to a Laravel app. Every symbol, path, and line number below was grepped and read directly in a checkout of that tree — nothing is quoted from memory or blog folklore.

The whole runtime in one picture: a server-specific SAPI plugs into a process-wide startup and a per-request cycle; each request compiles (or fetches cached) bytecode and runs it in the Zend VM over 16-byte zval cells.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The engine never talks to Apache, nginx, or your terminal directly. It calls a C vtable, sapi_module_struct, with slots for startup, activation, POST reading, cookie reading, and header sending — see sapi_module_struct, L230. CLI, FPM, and the embed SAPI are different implementations of that one interface.
  • There are two clocks. php_module_startup runs once per process and is MINIT in disguise: php_module_startup, L2169 copies the chosen SAPI in, boots the engine, and loads extensions. php_request_startup runs per request and is RINIT: php_request_startup, L1853 resets the compiler and executor, activates the SAPI, and calls each extension’s RINIT hook.
  • The compile step is a function pointer, not a hard-wired call: zend_compile_file, L90. That indirection is how OPcache — which assigns persistent_compile_file, L2238 to that pointer at startup — intercepts every script load without patching the engine.
  • Inside that default compile path, a re2c lexer and a bison parser meet: zendparse, L38 consumes scanner tokens and builds a Zend AST, which zend_compile_top_stmt, L12508 walks to emit opcodes.
  • The resulting bytecode is a zend_op_array, and running it is a two-hop: zend_execute_script, L1971 compiles and then hands the op_array to zend_execute, L116032, which pushes a top-level frame and enters the loop.
  • The interpreter itself is one huge generated function, execute_ex, L107065, that dispatches opcode after opcode; the file is generated from a definition file by Zend/zend_vm_gen.php, hence the dozens of operand-type specializations per handler.
  • Every value it touches is a 16-byte cell, struct _zval_struct, L341: a value union, a type tag, and a scratch union. Strings, arrays, and objects carry a zend_refcounted_h, L368 header whose refcount is bumped by GC_ADDREF, L866.
  • The JIT is not a separate engine. Function-mode compilation happens through zend_jit_op_array, L3364 when OPcache loads a script; tracing mode rides the VM’s own interrupt check, ZEND_VM_INTERRUPT_CHECK, L4367, recording hot loops via zend_jit_trace_execute, L732.

The detail view: follow one request from do_php_cli down through MINIT and RINIT, into the lexer/parser/compiler stage, and into the dispatch loop with its handlers, frames, zvals, and JIT hooks.

The SAPI Contract: One Engine, Many Servers

The cleanest place to enter the codebase is the question “what is a PHP server, really?” The answer is a struct of function pointers. main/SAPI.h declares sapi_module_struct, L230 with startup/shutdown and activate/deactivate pairs, read_post and read_cookies for input, and ub_write for output. A SAPI fills this vtable and registers it; the rest of the engine only ever calls through the abstraction.

The CLI is the smallest complete example. sapi/cli/php_cli.c defines cli_sapi_module, L407, whose startup slot calls php_module_startup, and whose entry point do_php_cli, L1187 parses options, starts the module, and drives the request cycle once per script argument. FPM and the Apache handler live in sibling directories under sapi/ and differ only in which callbacks they implement — one reads a FastCGI socket, the other an Apache connection.

That separation has a concrete consequence: request state lives in SAPI-owned globals, engine state in engine-owned globals, and the handoff happens at explicit functions like sapi_activate, L405, which primes request info and headers before execution starts.

MINIT and RINIT: Two Clocks, One Process

php_module_startup at main/main.c, L2169 is the MINIT phase every extension author knows. It stores the SAPI module, calls zend_startup, L930 to boot the engine’s globals and memory manager, loads INI files, and runs each extension’s startup function — the ones written with the ZEND_MODULE_STARTUP_N macro in Zend/zend_API.h. Whatever is registered here survives the whole process lifetime.

The request clock is different. php_request_startup, L1853 performs the per-request reset: it calls zend_activate, L1333 to re-initialize the compiler, executor, and scanner state, then sapi_activate, L405 to pick up request metadata, then zend_activate_modules, L3455 to run every extension’s RINIT — the hook that populates super-globals like $_SERVER. If you have read our Ruby tour, note the contrast: Ruby accumulates state across requests in one long-lived VM, while PHP deliberately tears everything down.

Shutdown is the mirror image, documented with explicit numbered steps in the source: php_request_shutdown, L1943 calls register_shutdown_function callbacks, runs destructors, flushes output buffers, resets timers, runs RSHUTDOWN through zend_deactivate_modules, sends headers, destroys super-globals, and deactivates the compiler and executor. Twelve steps, commented step by step.

From Source to Opcodes: the Lexer, the Parser, the Compiler

Compilation starts in an unusual place: the lexer grammar file. Zend/zend_language_scanner.l contains the default implementation of the compile hook, compile_file, L654, which first runs open_file_for_scanning, L529 to prime the re2c-generated lexer. Then zend_compile, L633 calls the bison parser zendparse, L38, whose grammar lives in Zend/zend_language_parser.y and builds a Zend AST. The walk ends in zend_compile_top_stmt, L12508, the top of the compiler that emits opcodes into an op_array.

The output data structures are compact. One instruction is struct _zend_op at Zend/zend_compile.h, L137: a handler pointer, three operand slots, an opcode number, and a line number. A whole function or script is struct _zend_op_array at L533, holding the opcode array, literals, variable info, and a try/catch table. These are the same op_arrays OPcache serializes into shared memory, so cached and freshly compiled code are structurally identical, not merely equivalent.

One drift note: older material references zend_execute_scripts(), but UPGRADING.INTERNALS records that it was removed; the entry point is now zend_execute_script, L1971, which compiles the file, calls zend_execute, and destroys the op_array afterwards unless OPcache has taken custody of it. The same separation of bytecode compiler from evaluator exists in CPython — but PHP compiles per request by default, exactly the cost OPcache erases.

Inside the Execute Loop: Frames, Handlers, and zvals

zend_execute, L116032 pushes a top-level call frame — a struct _zend_execute_data at Zend/zend_compile.h, L646 holding the current opline, the function, compiled variables, and a return value — then calls execute_ex, L107065. That function is the interpreter: you can see its hybrid dispatch table laid out as arrays of label addresses, one specialization per operand-type combination.

Handlers are best read in the definition file they are generated from. Assignment is opcode 22: ZEND_ASSIGN, L2835 writes one zval into another, with copy-on-write logic that calls GC_ADDREF when values are shared. The hot call path is opcode 60: ZEND_DO_FCALL, L4340, a ZEND_VM_HOT_HANDLER, pushes the callee’s frame and enters it. Return is opcode 62: ZEND_RETURN, L4545 copies the result back and leaves the frame. This frame-pushing model is what makes recursion and Node-style deep async stacks structurally similar at the VM level, even though the languages differ completely.

The value model underneath is brutally simple. A zval is 16 bytes: the union at struct _zval_struct, L341 stores the raw value, u1 stores the active type, and u2 is a scratch field reused for hash chains, argument counts, and line numbers. Anything bigger or mutable — strings at zend_string, L379, arrays, objects — lives behind a pointer to a refcounted block headed by zend_refcounted_h, and most assignments flow through GC_ADDREF, L866 or its decrement twin. The VM’s interrupt check at ZEND_VM_INTERRUPT_CHECK, L4367 enforces execution timeouts — and is the same hook the tracing JIT borrows to record hot loops, compiled by zend_jit_trace_execute, L732 from the opcache.jit=tracing mode accepted in zend_jit.c, L3751.

From Install to Your First Model

Building the engine from source is approachable, and the repository’s own README is the authority. For a minimal build from Git you need autoconf, bison, and re2c; a default build additionally wants libxml2 and libsqlite3. On Ubuntu that is one apt install line, on Fedora dnf, on macOS a single brew install. Then: ./buildconf to generate configure, ./configure --enable-debug for a development build (or plain ./configure for production), and make -j4, matching the job count to your core count from nproc.

After the build, make test runs the extensive .phpt suite that ships in-tree. Then you can watch the whole architecture in one command: the CLI binary you just compiled is cli_sapi_module made flesh, and running a script drives do_php_cli through module startup, one php_execute_script call — visible at main/main.c, L2674 — and the full twelve-step shutdown. What you get is a working PHP and a working mental model: you know which clock ran which function while your script printed one line.

Honest Limits

A few scope statements, each checkable in the tree. First, this tour follows the CLI SAPI path because it is the shortest complete cycle; FPM and Apache2handler implement the same vtable but their request plumbing was not walked here — their presence under sapi/ is verifiable, the details are not claimed. Second, Zend/zend_vm_execute.h is a generated artifact: Zend/zend_vm_gen.php states in its header that it creates that file from zend_vm_def.h, so line numbers in the generated file move when it is regenerated; the definition file is the stable reference. Third, the tracing JIT’s trigger is tied to the VM interrupt path as shown, but the code-generation backends differ per architecture, and zend_jit.c itself documents limits — it refuses opcache.jit changes at runtime when JIT is disabled, and caps JIT buffer sizes on AArch64 and x86_64. Finally, line numbers cited here match master at the time of writing; treat them as pointers into a moving tree, not permanent addresses.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of php/php-src showing how the SAPI interface, the MINIT/RINIT lifecycle, the re2c/bison compiler stage, the Zend VM execute loop, zvals, and the opcache JIT turn a .php file into executed opcodes.

entry.title: Inside ruby/ruby: How YARV Actually Runs Your Code

link.title: Inside ruby/ruby: How YARV Actually Runs Your Code

entry.content:
Every Rails developer eventually meets the same mystery: the first request after boot is slow, and every request after that is fine. Part of that warm-up is Ruby quietly filling method call caches. When foo.bar executes, the interpreter records which class it found the method on and which C handler will invoke it — and the next call skips the entire superclass walk. Delete that bookkeeping and Ruby would feel like a different language; it is the reason each, map, and your controller actions can afford to be plain method calls.

A second mystery is the gap between typing ruby app.rb and seeing your first line run. Your source is parsed by a real parser, compiled into bytecode for a register-based virtual machine, laid out into stack frames, and only then does execution begin. None of this is visible from the language surface, yet every performance question — why some allocations are cheap, why threads switch when they do — answers to it.

This post is a source tour of ruby/ruby at branch master (commit c0013b358f59, checked out 2026-11-10). Rather than listing features, we follow one execution path: startup, parsing, compilation, bytecode dispatch, method resolution, garbage collection, and concurrency. Every file, symbol, and line number below was grep-verified against that exact tree before publication; where the tree has drifted from folklore — and it has — we say so.

The Ruby execution path from left to right: two parser frontends converge on one bytecode compiler, whose output runs inside the YARV interpreter loop, with method dispatch, garbage collection, and thread scheduling hanging off the same execution context.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Startup is a straight C chain: main calls ruby_run_node(ruby_options(argc, argv)) at main.c, L42, ruby_options parses argv and builds the VM stack, and the returned <main> iseq eventually reaches rb_iseq_eval_main from rb_ec_exec_node (eval.c, L292). There is no separate “script loader”: the same path runs irb, rails runner, and your one-liner.
  • Prism is now the default frontend. version.c, L194 defines RB_DEFAULT_PARSER as RB_DEFAULT_PARSER_PRISM, and the rb_ruby_prism_p macro branches on it all over the tree. The legacy LALR grammar in parse.y — lexer at parser_yylex, L10488 — is still selectable via --parser=parse.y (ruby.c, L373).
  • Both frontends produce bytecode through iseq.c: the Prism path is pm_iseq_build, which calls prepare_iseq_build and then pm_iseq_compile_node, L1245; the parse.y path reaches rb_iseq_compile_node the same way, via rb_iseq_new_with_opt at iseq.c, L1199. Downstream, nothing knows which frontend produced an iseq.
  • The compiler’s real body is the giant switch iseq_compile_each0, L11139, walking NODEs into linked instruction lists, cleaned afterwards by iseq_peephole_optimize when peephole_optimization is on (compile.c, L4652).
  • YARV’s inner loop is vm_exec_core: it pins pc and cfp to machine registers — on x86_64 they live in %r14 and %r15 (vm_exec.c, L50) — and jumps through dispatch tables generated from insns.def (vm_exec.c, L94). Instructions themselves are tiny C bodies like putobject and branchif.
  • A method call is one instruction, opt_send_without_block, L902, which hands a CALL_DATA to vm_sendish; the probe that decides whether the cached entry is still valid is vm_cc_hit_p.
  • Dispatch and GC hang off the same execution context: lookups consult a per-class cache (callable_method_entry_or_negative, L2132), and GC.start is a thin Primitive into the pluggable engine in gc/default/default.c.
  • Concurrency is not a separate subsystem: branchif calls RUBY_VM_CHECK_INTS between instructions, which is exactly how signals, thread switches, and interrupts get their chance to run.

The detail view adds the machinery behind each stage: option handling, both compile paths, cache population under the VM lock, incremental mark steps, lazy sweeping, heap page allocation, and the fiber switch path.

Two parsers, one bytecode compiler

The interesting design decision in current master is that Ruby carries two complete frontends and guarantees they emit the same downstream artifact. Prism parses your script in prism_script when the default holds; otherwise process_options (ruby.c, L2375) routes to the LALR machinery, where yycompile drives yyparse over tokens from parser_yylex. What both produce is not shared code but a shared contract: an iseq built by iseq.c, using the same prepare_iseq_build prologue and the same instruction set.

Compilation is where the AST dies and bytecode is born. The parse.y compiler is compile.c’s recursive walk: rb_iseq_compile_node at compile.c, L901 dispatches into iseq_compile_each0 per NODE type, appending instructions like putobject into a linked anchor, then the peephole pass repairs jump chains. The Prism compiler mirrors this shape in prism_compile.c, from pm_compile_node, L8803 downward — same target instruction sequence, different source tree. If you have read our CPython tour, the contrast is instructive: Python 3.13 keeps one parser with optional speed-ups, while Ruby runs two real frontends behind one bytecode format.

Inside vm_exec_core: frames, insns, interrupts

The interpreter loop is deliberately unremarkable C. vm_exec (vm.c, L2891) pushes a tag, tries the JIT entry first, and otherwise calls vm_exec_core; exceptions unwind through vm_exec_loop and vm_exec_handle_exception before re-entering the core. The core itself is one function that never returns between instructions: pc and the control frame pointer are register-pinned, and INSN_DISPATCH is a computed-goto over labels generated from insns.def. The fallback call-threaded variant, a plain switch loop, exists in the same file (vm_exec.c, L122).

Frames are just slices of one contiguous VM stack. The struct at rb_control_frame_t, L956 carries pc, sp, the iseq pointer, self, and the environment pointer ep — seven fields, no allocation per call. That is why Ruby frame pushes are cheap and why caller walks the stack instead of a heap list. The instruction definitions themselves show how far the economy goes: putobject has a body that is literally an empty comment block, because its operand — the immediate value to push — is stored inside the encoded instruction stream and the VM’s register conventions do the rest. Branch instructions double as safe points: branchif runs RUBY_VM_CHECK_INTS (insns.def, L1270) so the interpreter can honor a signal or a timer between jumps without a dedicated polling instruction. Anything that might allocate, raise, or block is marked non-leaf in the same definitions, which is how the loop stays interruptible without checking on every single opcode.

The call cache: method calls that remember

Every foo.bar compiles to a send instruction carrying a CALL_DATA — an immutable rb_callinfo (name, flags, arity) plus a mutable rb_callcache slot. The cache entry records the receiver class, the resolved method entry, and a C call handler. At runtime vm_sendish calls vm_search_method_fastpath: if vm_cc_hit_p sees the same class and the method entry was not invalidated, the cached handler is tail-called directly — no method table touch at all.

On a miss, vm_populate_cc takes the VM lock, resolves the method through rb_callable_method_entry, and stores a fresh cache entry with vm_cc_new (vm_insnhelper.c, L2151) into a per-class table; under OPT_INLINE_METHOD_CACHE the result is also written back into the call site itself (vm_insnhelper.c, L2318). The per-class layer has its own lock-free fast read (vm_method.c, L2151) and even caches failures — a method that does not exist becomes a negative_cme — which is why method_missing misses stay cheap. Redefining a method flips invalidation bits through vm_cme_invalidate, and vm_call_method (vm_insnhelper.c, L5128) then re-specializes the handler per method type in vm_call_method_each_type — ISEQ, CFUNC, IVAR, BMETHOD, ZSUPER, REFINED. This is the warm-up tax Rails pays at boot so steady-state requests do not; other dynamic frameworks re-resolve lookups differently, but Ruby’s cache is inline in the bytecode stream itself.

GC and concurrency: pages, steps, switches

GC.start is, remarkably, Ruby code: gc.rb, L65 forwards to Primitive.gc_start_internal (gc.c, L4387), which dispatches through a modular function table (rb_gc_function_map_t, L766) to the default engine in gc/default/default.c. The engine grows the heap in fixed pages (heap_page_allocate, L3003) carved into slots sized by RVALUE_SLOT_SIZE — the old one-union-fits-all RVALUE layout is gone; slot geometry is now explicit, and allocation walks a per-page free list rather than picking objects out of one giant union. Marking runs incrementally with a per-cycle budget (gc_marks_step, L8134), spreading gc_mark_children work across short pauses, and sweeping is lazy (gc_sweep_step, L5871), amortized over later allocations. The practical consequence is the one every Rails operator knows from profiling: stop-the-world pauses are not the norm, because a mark step can end mid-cycle and resume after the mutator runs more instructions.

Threads and fibers share the safe-point story. Thread.new reaches rb_thread_create and starts in thread_start_func_2; switching happens in rb_thread_schedule, where rb_thread_schedule_limits yields the current thread once running_time_us exceeds its slice (thread.c, L1682), saving machine context and handing off through the per-Ractor scheduler. Fibers are cheaper: fiber_switch swaps stack contexts, entered via rb_fiber_transfer, and a first resume starts the body in rb_fiber_start. If you run Ruby workloads on Redis or Postgres-backed services, this is the layer your async drivers ride on.

From Install to Your First Model

Everything above can be reproduced from a checkout. Per the repo’s own docs: clone with git clone https://github.com/ruby/ruby.git (README.md, L43), generate the build system with ./autogen.sh (building_ruby.md, L94), configure into a prefix such as ../configure --prefix="${HOME}/.rubies/ruby-master" (building_ruby.md, L115), then make (building_ruby.md, L124) and make install (building_ruby.md, L132). The tree’s own test suite runs with make test-all -j8 (building_ruby.md, L201). From there, ruby -e 'puts RubyVM::InstructionSequence.compile("1+1").disasm' shows you the same bytecode vm_exec_core executes, and --parser=parse.y lets you diff both frontends’ output. Building your first model on top — a Rack app, an ORM class — then exercises exactly the dispatch and GC paths diagrammed above, the same ones your Rails app hits in production.

Honest Limits

  • This tour describes the interpreter path only. YJIT and ZJIT live in the same tree (yjit.c, zjit.c) and hook the same call sites we visited, but we verified none of their codegen internals here.
  • Line numbers are pinned to master at commit c0013b358f59; Ruby moves fast, and symbols like vm_sendish have been reshaped repeatedly in recent years.
  • The GC engine is pluggable in-tree: besides gc/default/default.c, the repo carries an mmtk binding. We covered the default engine only, and no performance numbers in this post are benchmarks — they are structural facts from the source.
